neet_phy_u17_t01_1.working: Hertz found that ultraviolet light falling on the spark-gap electrodes made high-voltage sparks pass more easily. This was the first hint of photoemission.

neet_phy_u17_t01_2.working: At fixed frequency, more intensity means more photons, so more photoelectrons and a higher saturation current. The maximum kinetic energy depends only on frequency, so the stopping potential is unchanged.

neet_phy_u17_t01_3.working: Since 1.5ν0 is above threshold, each photon is absorbed in a single event. Emission is therefore practically instantaneous (about 1e-9 s or less), however dim the light.

neet_phy_u17_t01_4.working: Saturation current rises with intensity (A-I). Stopping potential depends on frequency and metal, not intensity (B-II). Threshold frequency is a property of the metal alone (C-III). Time lag is practically zero (D-IV).

neet_phy_u17_t01_5.working: A is true: alkali metals respond to visible light. B is true: Zn and Mg need UV. C is true: wave theory predicts KE rising with intensity. D is false: curves at the same frequency share one stopping potential. E is true: higher frequency gives a larger stopping potential with about the same saturation current.
